title: Same songs, different hits
hook: When people copy each other's picks, does the best song still rise to the top?

knows: that some songs are better liked than others
doesNotKnow: that when people follow what others chose, the same songs end up with very different outcomes in different worlds

misconception: The best song will always rise to the top; a hit is a sign of quality alone.
objective: The learner can explain that when each pick makes a song more likely to be picked again, early luck compounds: the same songs give a big but different hit in each world and the best song can finish near the bottom, while without copying the outcome is stable and close to quality.

claims.text: In the lesson's 8 worlds (seeds 1 to 8, rule on the stage), with copying on the best song finishes 3rd, 1st, 7th, 1st, 4th, 1st, 1st, 3rd after 1,000 listeners, so its lowest finish is 7th (world 3); with copying off, same seeds and same draws, it finishes 2nd, 1st, 2nd, 1st, 2nd, 1st, 2nd, 1st, so its lowest finish is 2nd.
claims.source: Builder's node re-run 2026-10-14 of exactly the Demo.tsx rule (mulberry32(k) for world k; one u per listener; first song whose cumulative interval holds u x sum(w); finish = 1 + songs with strictly more picks). World 3 with copying: picks 33, 40, 7, 38, 214, 158, 482, 28. No ties for the best song's place in any of the 16 worlds. Matches the brief and the spec. Seeds 1 to 8 are the first eight, not searched for this result; robustness (spec, 500 blocks of 8 worlds, seeds 1000 + 8b + j): copying on, lowest finish 5th or lower in 70.2% of blocks, 7th or 8th in 36.8%; off, 4th or higher in 98.2%. So 7th is a fairly lucky-to-show draw, not the typical worst case. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1, session 2): Own re-run (scratchpad fc2/songs.mjs) that extracts APPEAL and simulate() verbatim from Demo.tsx and mulberry32 from src/kit/random.ts: copying on finishes 3,1,7,1,4,1,1,3; off 2,1,2,1,2,1,2,1; world 3 picks 33,40,7,38,214,158,482,28; no ties with the best song in any of the 16 worlds. Robustness (seeds 1000+8b+j, 500 blocks): on lowest >=5th 70.2%, >=7th 36.8%; off <=4th 98.2%. Matches. Predict answer "7th of 8" and the reveal (computed from RUNS) agree.

claims.text: After 1,000 listeners the top song in each world takes 35-48% of the picks with copying on (34.9, 38.7, 48.2, 46.3, 36.9, 44.5, 42.9, 43.9%) and 15-18% with copying off (15.5, 16.5, 16.0, 16.9, 14.7, 16.9, 17.6, 17.4%), so no song is above 18% without copying.
claims.source: Same node re-run as c1 (2026-10-14). The reveal computes the range from the stage's own runs and rounds to whole percent. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1, session 2): Same re-run: top shares on 34.9,38.7,48.2,46.3,36.9,44.5,42.9,43.9% (rounds to 35-48%); off 15.5,16.5,16.0,16.9,14.7,16.9,17.6,17.4% (rounds to 15-18%; max 17.6% < 18, so "no song above 18%" holds). Reveal computes both from the stage runs.

claims.text: In the model, 8 songs have appeal 1.0, 1.1, ..., 1.7 (the best 70% more appealing than the worst); each of 1,000 listeners in turn picks a song with chance proportional to appeal x (1 + earlier picks of that song) with copying on, or to appeal only with copying off.
claims.source: Modelling choice from the brief (company/domains/briefs/probability.chance.md, NCM batch 1 #3) and spec; stated on the stage rule line and in the predict question; identical in Demo.tsx (APPEAL, simulate). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1, session 2): Demo.tsx APPEAL = [1..1.7], w = a*(1+p[i]) or a, pick by cumulative interval of u*sum(w): proportional to the weight as stated. 1.7/1.0 = 70% more. ADVISORY (not blocking): the stage rule line reads "Pick chance = appeal x (1 + earlier picks)", which is a weight, not a chance (it exceeds 1 after one pick). Suggest "Pick chance proportional to appeal x (1 + earlier picks)" or "Pick weight = ...".

claims.text: Copying on and copying off use the same 8 seeds and the same random draw for each listener, so only the pick rule differs between the two sets of worlds.
claims.source: Property of the code: Demo.tsx simulate(seed, copy) draws exactly one u = rng() per listener from mulberry32(seed) in both modes. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1, session 2): Code read: simulate() calls r() exactly once per listener in both modes, before the copy branch; same seed k+1 for world k in RUNS.on and RUNS.off.

claims.text: In the copying worlds an early pick makes a song more likely to be picked again, so early leads compound: in world 3 the best song is already 7th after 100 listeners and stays 7th; quality still tilts the odds (the best song wins 4 of the 8 copying worlds) but does not decide the hit.
claims.source: Reveal paragraph 2. Node re-run 2026-10-14, copying on, best-song finishes at 100 / 200 / 300 / 500 / 1,000 listeners: world 3 is 7th at every checkpoint; finishes at 1,000 are 1st in worlds 2, 4, 6, 7. The brief reports the best song wins about 45% of copying worlds over 2,000 worlds. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1, session 2): Same re-run, copying on, best-song finish at 100..1,000: world 3 is 7th at all 10 checkpoints; best wins worlds 2,4,6,7 (4 of 8). "Quality tilts the odds": best wins 42.9% of copying worlds (seeds 1-2,000) and 43.3% (seeds 1,000-4,999) vs 12.5% for an equal song. Note: the source's "about 45%" (brief) is 43% in my runs; not learner-facing.

claims.text: The lesson is a toy model with made-up appeal numbers, not a measurement of any real market.
claims.source: Reveal caveat. The toy does not reproduce the MusicLab study (48 songs, many listeners) and the lesson does not say it does. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1, session 2): Reveal caveat text matches; the lesson never cites MusicLab to learners (grep of Demo.tsx). True of the model (appeal values are invented constants).

claims.text: NOT SHOWN TO LEARNERS until a human source check: Salganik, Dodds and Watts (2006) found that when participants could see others' downloads, success was more unequal and less predictable, but the best songs rarely did very badly and the worst rarely did very well.
claims.source: Salganik, Dodds & Watts (2006), 'Experimental study of inequality and unpredictability in an artificial cultural market', Science 311(5762): 854-856. NEEDS A HUMAN SOURCE CHECK (brief claim 4); do not quote study sizes or percentages until checked. Kept out of all learner text by instruction. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1, session 2): Not in learner text. Citation confirmed via search-quoted abstract and records: Salganik MJ, Dodds PS, Watts DJ (2006) Science 311(5762): 854-856, doi 10.1126/science.1121066; 14,341 participants; abstract: more social influence increased both inequality and unpredictability of success; the best songs rarely did poorly and the worst rarely did well, but any other result was possible. Claim text matches the abstract. Primary PDF unreachable (proxy DNS-fails uvm.edu, toronto.edu), so medium confidence. If shown to learners later, keep to the abstract wording; do not add numbers unchecked.

recall.question: The same 8 new products launch in two separate towns where buyers can see what others bought. What is most likely?
options: The best product wins in both towns, because quality decides
Each town gets a big winner, but not always the same one
No product pulls far ahead in either town
recall.why: When buyers copy earlier buyers, early luck compounds: each town locks onto its own early leader, which takes a big share. Quality tilts the odds but does not decide the winner.

references.note: rich-get-richer and the unpredictability of popularity; section unconfirmed (brief says 18.3-18.4)
